content:
Quick answer: Joint and muscle aches can occur during perimenopause and menopause, but new pain is not automatically caused by hormones. HRT is used for menopause symptoms after an individual discussion of benefits and risks. It is not an established treatment for arthritis, and research does not show a reliable joint-pain benefit for everyone.

Why joint symptoms need a separate assessment

The NHS lists muscle aches and joint pains among menopause symptoms. Sleep problems, mood changes and other symptoms may happen at the same time. However, osteoarthritis, inflammatory arthritis, injury and other illnesses can also cause pain in midlife.

You cannot reliably distinguish these causes from an online checklist. Arrange a GP assessment if pain affects normal activities or sleep, keeps returning, worsens or has not improved after two weeks of self-care. Mention visible swelling and prolonged morning stiffness. Do not wait for menopause treatment to resolve symptoms that may need a different assessment.

NICE NG100 recommends specialist referral for suspected persistent joint inflammation. Referral should not be delayed while waiting for blood test results. This rheumatoid arthritis guidance is separate from menopause care.

What NICE recommends HRT for

NICE NG23, recommendation 1.5.1, recommends offering HRT for menopause-related hot flushes and sweats. Other menopause symptoms have their own treatment options. The discussion should cover your symptoms, preferences, medical history and the benefits and risks of the particular treatment.

Systemic HRT replaces oestrogen. If you still have a womb, a progestogen is usually needed as well to protect its lining. Local vaginal oestrogen is a different treatment for vaginal and urinary symptoms; it is not a joint-pain treatment. Your prescriber can explain which option, if any, is suitable.

Does HRT improve joint pain?

The evidence is mixed. A post-hoc analysis of the Women's Health Initiative trial found a modest reduction in joint-pain frequency with one oral oestrogen-only regimen in women who had previously had a hysterectomy. That finding does not establish that every form of HRT works for every person with joint pain.

A 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis found inconsistent results across studies and no clear overall benefit for generalised musculoskeletal pain. The studies differed in treatment, population and outcomes. The review could not draw firm conclusions about HRT for these symptoms.

HRT should not be presented as a way to repair cartilage, control rheumatoid arthritis or replace arthritis treatment. Discuss the whole menopause picture with your GP rather than starting treatment on a promise that it will relieve joint pain.

Benefits and risks depend on the person and treatment

The NHS HRT benefits and risks guide explains that age, symptoms, medical history, type of HRT and duration of use matter. HRT can relieve menopause symptoms and helps protect against osteoporosis while it is taken.

Oral HRT increases the risk of blood clots. Standard transdermal HRT, such as patches, gel or spray, does not increase venous clot risk in the same way. This does not mean it is automatically suitable if you have had a clot, have antiphospholipid antibodies or have another important risk factor. Ask for an individual assessment rather than choosing a route yourself.

Breast cancer history and risk also affect the decision. Systemic HRT is usually not advised after breast cancer. Local vaginal treatment is a separate discussion that may involve your cancer specialist. Do not treat general HRT information as permission to use it during or after cancer treatment.

If you already have a rheumatic condition

Rheumatoid arthritis: tell your GP and rheumatology team about both menopause symptoms and changes in joint symptoms. Neither a menopause diagnosis nor improvement on HRT proves that inflammatory disease is controlled. Do not change prescribed arthritis medicines yourself.

Lupus or antiphospholipid antibodies: obtain specialist advice before considering systemic HRT. EULAR's women's health recommendations support carefully selected use for severe menopause hot flushes and sweats in people with stable or inactive lupus and negative antiphospholipid antibodies. Positive antibodies require particular assessment of clot and cardiovascular risks. This is not a blanket statement that HRT is safe with lupus or antiphospholipid syndrome.

Osteoarthritis: use a separate care plan for joint pain and function. NICE NG226 supports tailored therapeutic exercise and, for people living with overweight or obesity, support with weight management. HRT is not a substitute for that care.

Ask a pharmacist or prescriber to check your exact medicines, supplements and proposed HRT. A general article cannot confirm compatibility. The NHS medicines guide explains that HRT and other medicines can affect each other.

Bone health and daily activity

Menopause increases the risk of osteoporosis. Long-term steroid treatment can add to fracture risk. Ask your GP whether you need a bone-health assessment, particularly if you have had a fracture or take steroids. HRT is one possible part of menopause care, not the only osteoporosis treatment.

Discuss activity that fits your symptoms and ability, including strength and weight-bearing activity where suitable. A balanced diet, adequate calcium and vitamin D, not smoking and avoiding excess alcohol also support bone health. The NHS osteoporosis guide explains assessment and treatment. A physiotherapist can help adapt exercise if joint pain limits it.

Preparing for an appointment

Write down when pain started, any swelling, how long morning stiffness lasts, how symptoms affect sleep and daily life, and any changes in periods or other menopause symptoms. Bring a list of medicines and supplements. You can ask:

  • Does my joint pain need a separate arthritis assessment?
  • Which menopause treatments fit my symptoms and medical history?
  • Do I need a medicine-interaction or bone-health review?
  • What symptoms should prompt urgent help?

In England, an HRT prescription prepayment certificate can reduce prescription costs for eligible HRT medicines. It does not cover every HRT medicine or all other prescriptions. Check eligibility and what it covers before buying.

When joint pain needs urgent help

Seek urgent medical advice for sudden severe joint pain, difficulty moving or bearing weight, or a hot, swollen joint, even without fever. Do not assume it is menopause or an ordinary arthritis flare. In England, Scotland and Wales, contact an urgent GP service or call 111. In Northern Ireland, contact your GP or GP out-of-hours service. See NHS septic arthritis advice.

After an injury, severe joint pain, inability to walk or put weight on a joint, or a joint that has moved out of place needs A&E assessment. See NHS joint pain advice.

Common questions

Can menopause cause joint pain?

Joint and muscle aches are recognised symptoms, but other causes may coexist. New, persistent or swollen joints need assessment rather than an assumption about hormones.

Will HRT help my joints?

Some studies suggest a modest benefit with particular treatments, while wider evidence is inconsistent. There is no reliable promise of relief, and HRT is not an arthritis treatment.

Can I use HRT with rheumatoid arthritis?

Suitability depends on your symptoms, medical history, medicines and risk factors. Ask your GP and rheumatology team to review the exact treatment. This article cannot give a blanket yes.

Is transdermal HRT automatically safe with lupus or clotting risk?

No. Route is only one part of the decision. Lupus activity, antiphospholipid antibodies, previous clots and other risk factors need specialist assessment.
